title: Forming the Affections of Our Children
author: Paul Kearney
summary: Paul Kearney, a former classical-school elementary teacher and now a father, tells how his three-year-old son responded to a mountain view by asking for the Emily Dickinson poem about statures touching the sky. The moment convinced him that poetry memorized in early childhood becomes part of how a child perceives reality, even before he understands the words. He argues that children can encounter beauty and feel delight before grasping concepts, and that delight precedes meaning. In his view the purpose of memorizing poems with small children is not performance but to have poetry arise unbidden when reality calls for it. Because young children are malleable, their tastes can be deliberately formed, and if parents leave it to chance, competing voices will form their souls. He concludes that parents, especially of sons, have a duty to show children what is truly worth having in their repertoire of knowledge and experience.
points: A three-year-old reaching for a Dickinson poem at a mountain overlook illustrates how early poetry becomes part of a child's lived experience of reality.
Children can delight in beauty before they understand the concepts behind it, so delight comes before meaning in formation.
The point of memorizing poetry with young children is for it to arise unbidden when reality calls for it, not for recitation as performance.
Children's tastes are malleable and can be formed deliberately, and leaving them to chance lets clamoring outside voices do the forming.
Parents have a duty to introduce children, and especially boys, to the simple beauties that enrich the soul, even amid the survival mode of ordinary family life.
quotes: Informed by our faith, we believe that beauty, truth, and goodness exist for their own sake, and the pursuit of these transcendentals is a gift.
Poetry had become part of his lived experience, and he reached for it when no other form of communication could do justice to what he was seeing.
Yet once in a while, children reveal the work that years of formation have been quietly striving to accomplish.
Children are capable of encountering beauty before they understand the concepts behind beauty. My son did not understand the Dickinson poem, but he did not need to understand it.

Perhaps the point of memorizing poetry for young children is not so that they can recite it on command and impress their friends and relatives. Perhaps it is for poetry to arise unbidden when reality calls for it.

Their taste is something that can be formed deliberately, and if we simply leave their taste up to the vagaries of life, plenty of clamoring voices will chime in to grab their attention and form their souls.
Parents of young children, and especially of young men, have a duty to show them what is truly worth having in their repertoire of knowledge and experience.
